EN: A unique world, Kerbin has flat plains, soaring mountains and wide, blue \noceans. Home to the kerbals, it has just the right conditions to support a vast, \nseemingly undepletable population of the eager green creatures.
Reaching a stable orbit around Kerbin is one of the first things budding space \nprograms strive for. It is said that a kerbal who can get their ship into orbit is \nhalfway to anywhere.
There are two moons circling Kerbin: the Mun, which is a nearby trip for the \nadventurous, and Minmus... seems minty fresh somehow.
Scientists speculate about possible ways to make it "Awesome like in the \nstories." Some of those ideas have led to new breakthroughs in aerospace \ntechnology.
Moho figures in kerbal mythology as a fiery place with oceans of flowing \nlava. In reality, however, it's much less interesting.

The solar system consists of seven planets and nine moons. Kerbals have looked up since \nthe dawn of time to figure out just how to reach and explore every one of these shiny dots \nin the sky.
The Solar System

Discovering the amount of Ore is a little bit 
more challenging though.

You can only detect the amount of Ore an 
asteroid contains by getting up close to it, 
and then checking its properties. 

This means you have to rendezvous, before 
you know just how much Ore there might be.

One point of note when you drill Ore from an asteroid, it does reduce the mass of the asteroid. The Ore \nextracted adds mass to the mining vessel, so unless you discard the Ore after drilling you will have quite \na heavy vessel.
Every asteroid in the solar system has some amount of Ore in it. Generally speaking, the larger the \nasteroid, the more Ore there is.

Due to mining and conversion being long running processes, keeping resources flowing involves some \nstrategic thinking. It is never fun to come back and find out nothing happened in the last year. Here are \nsome things to keep in mind:
Managing the core heat of these parts is key to a long running operation. If the core heat cannot be maintained then efficency suffers. Optimal core heat is: Drills: 500K Converters: 1000K
When extracting Ore, or converting it to other resources, you must have room to \nstore the end product. If you are mining and converting then that means thinking \nabout storing two resources.
All that heat is going to go somewhere, usually throughout your vessel. It's likely \nyou will need to have a number of radiators on the vessel to manage heat.
These processes are very hungry for EC, so you need some \ngood EC sources (solar or fuel cells maybe) to back them.

To get the Ore out of the ground you will need to drill! Drills are Electric Charge (EC) hungry devices that \nextract Ore while generating lots of heat. This means that drilling requires a bit of thought and \nmanagement.
